<reason>B kept the debate anchored to the motion's actual category—resource-rich developing countries—and built a record-based case (Nigeria, Chad, Angola) that A's design-based "a fund can..." arguments never squarely rebutted. B's "strip out the word can" framing and the one-leak-point vs three-leak-points comparison were sharp, and B's handling of A's Chile counterexample (turning it into evidence that funds work only where institutions pre-exist, then noting A conceded "no guaranteed stopper" under capture) was the decisive move. A landed real pressure with Q2 on what finances services in a bust, and rightly exposed B's "ordinary tax base" answer as thin; but B's reply that Nigeria borrowed anyway having also lost its fund blunted the force, since A never showed why the expected value of a fund beats cash where capture is likely. Minor costs to B: a clipped rebuttal and nonstandard reference tags. Overall B made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 A1/A2: reclaiming Chile as "my witness, not PRO's" by pointing to its independent central bank, fiscal rule, and courts, then quoting A's own concession that once a president captures legislature and courts "there is no guaranteed stopper," and noting that Nigeria borrowed in the bust anyway despite having had a fund—collapsing A's cushion argument on A's own framework.</best_rebuttal>
